summary: MassDOT's Interim Policy for the Use of UAS (dated September 6, 2017) centralizes UAS authority under the Aeronautics Division ("MassDOT Aeronautics") for all MassDOT and MBTA divisions. jurisdiction_name: Massachusetts (arising from the City of Newton; decided by the federal District of Massachusetts)
geographic_scope: Statewide precedent (case arose from a municipal ordinance in Newton, Massachusetts, but the preemption analysis is of general application within the District of Massachusetts)
issuing_authority: United States District Court, District of Massachusetts
citation: Singer v. City of Newton, No. 1:17-cv-10071-WGY (D. Mass. Sept. 21, 2017)
revision_date: Unknown — no indication of appeal or subsequent modification located in this pass
status: Current / in force (not appealed, per sources reviewed)
binding_level: Binding within the District of Massachusetts (federal trial-court decision); persuasive, not binding, outside that district

requirement_type: Judicial invalidation (conflict preemption) of specific local-ordinance provisions
aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to any AEC firm operating in a Massachusetts municipality with a local drone ordinance, since Massachusetts has no state preemption statute of its own and this remains the leading judicial authority on the state/local/federal boundary
summary: Dr. Michael Singer, an FAA-certificated recreational drone pilot, challenged four provisions of a December 2016 City of Newton ordinance: a local UAS-registration requirement and three flight-operation restrictions (a below-400-foot altitude ceiling over private property absent consent, a ban on flight over public property without permission, and a beyond-visual-line-of-sight restriction). Judge William G. Young held these four provisions were conflict-preempted because, in combination, they obstructed federal objectives and directly conflicted with FAA regulation of low-altitude navigable airspace; the court rejected a field-preemption theory but found conflict preemption as to all four challenged provisions. Unchallenged parts of the ordinance were left standing.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use the statewide rule as the regulatory baseline, while separately screening site-control rules and any local authority preserved by the preemption provision. Record that jurisdictional check in the project flight-planning package.

verification_status: The case caption, docket number (1:17-cv-10071), presiding judge (Young, J.), decision date (September 21, 2017), and holding (conflict preemption found on all four challenged provisions; field preemption rejected) were corroborated across the official GovInfo federal court-filing record and multiple independent secondary legal summaries (Holland & Knight, Steptoe, Harvard Law Review); the court's opinion text itself was not re-opened section-by-section from GovInfo's PACER-sourced PDF in this pass, so exact quoted language should be independently confirmed by counsel before citation in a dispositive filing.
notes: MATERIAL FINDING relevant to the state-preemption research category: unlike Maryland (which has an express statutory preemption provision, Md. Code Ann., Econ. Dev. §14-301), Massachusetts has enacted no state statute addressing whether counties or municipalities may regulate UAS. Singer v. City of Newton is the only identified authority bearing on the state/local/federal boundary for Massachusetts, and it rests entirely on federal conflict-preemption doctrine rather than any state preemption statute — meaning a Massachusetts municipality's drone ordinance is vulnerable to a federal preemption challenge on a provision-by-provision basis, but nothing in Massachusetts law itself forecloses a municipality from enacting one. AEC firms should still expect to encounter, and should independently check for, local drone ordinances in each Massachusetts municipality where they plan to operate.

summary: No Massachusetts state-court decision beyond Singer v. City of Newton (MA-004), Attorney General opinion, or currently operative gubernatorial executive order directly and dispositively addressing UAS regulation was located. No enacted Massachusetts statute imposing a state-agency UAS procurement, approved-manufacturer, or country-of-origin restriction was located. As of this research date, the most advanced pending measure is H.5444 ("Responsible Robotics Act"), which passed the House 155-1 on May 20, 2026 and would ban manufacturing, selling, possessing, or operating a weapon-mounted robot/UAS and impose a warrant requirement for law-enforcement use of a weaponized robotic device on private property or for surveillance/location tracking; it remained pending in the Senate Committee on Ways and Means as of the official bill-status page fetched for this research pass. Five additional bills addressing critical-facility no-fly zones (S.2454), school-overflight restrictions (H.3618), broad take-off/landing and night-flight restrictions (H.3663), UAS definitions/weaponization/surveillance (H.3749/S.2438), and a ban on sale of Chinese-manufactured drones (H.3800) remained pending before the Joint Committee on Transportation following a July 22, 2025 hearing, with no indication of further enactment identified in this pass.

AEC firms and counsel should not rely on any secondary source describing an enacted Massachusetts weaponized-drone statute under a "Chapter 190B" or similar citation; no such enacted provision currently exists.
